works.title: Trust but Verify: Implementing Frontier AI Policy in California and Beyond
works.venue: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
works.contribution: Kevin Wei: Main author of the “Foundations: AI Assessment & Evaluation” chapter
works.summary:
In the year since California’s Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act passed, also known as Senate Bill 53 (SB 53), artificial intelligence (AI) has made striking advances in areas ranging from mathematics to coding. At the same time, previous hypothetical risks posed by frontier AI systems have become serious, documented concerns. For example, models have found and exploited previously unknown software vulnerabilities and gained unauthorized access to external databases. As AI capabilities continue to improve, such incidents are likely to become more frequent and consequential.

Policymakers recognize the need to respond but face an evidence dilemma: AI evolves so quickly that responding prematurely risks entrenching ineffective policies, while delaying action could leave society vulnerable to serious risks. SB 53 aims to alleviate this dilemma by generating more evidence about AI risks to inform future policies. It trusts frontier AI companies, which hold much of the relevant technical expertise, to design and implement appropriate risk management practices and disclose the evidence behind them. In parallel, the approach empowers government bodies to verify industry claims about risks and the effectiveness of those practices. This “trust but verify” approach, first outlined in the California Report on Frontier AI Policy, combines flexibility with independent accountability.

This report aims to guide the implementation of “trust but verify” approaches such as SB 53 and maximize the chances they accomplish their goals. The design choices California makes at the beginning of implementation—such as which companies should be subject to these policies, how detailed frontier AI frameworks should be, and how to triage information about AI incidents—will ground how California manages risks for years to come.

These questions matter not just in California but also around the world as governments grapple with the challenge of how to govern advanced AI systems. SB 53 has already inspired similar frameworks in New York and Illinois. Even where “trust but verify” frameworks are not adopted in their entirety, many of the most important questions this report examines will remain relevant. For example, many governments will want to have confidence that models have undergone appropriate safety testing before they allow models to be deployed, or receive incident reports when models cause serious harm within their borders. As the federal government grapples with similar questions, California’s experiment in frontier AI governance and implementation can offer real-world evidence to support thoughtful federal policy.

SB 53 will not, and should not, be the final chapter in the story of how the United States governs advanced AI systems. California will need to strengthen its evaluation and assessment ecosystem, ensure that sufficient information on serious incidents is reported to the government, and respond to the novel challenges posed by potential recursive self-improvement—when AI fully automates AI R&D, potentially causing an intelligence explosion. However, it represents a critical first step that will inform the policies that follow. Given the profound uncertainty over the trajectory and pace of AI development, generating substantial evidence on AI’s capabilities and risks and developing a robust verification ecosystem can help policymakers make better decisions in the months and years to come.

works.title: FraudBench: A Legal Evaluation of AI Deception
works.venue: NeurIPS 2026 Datasets and Benchmarks Track
works.abstract: We introduce FraudBench, an evaluation of large language models' (LLMs) propensities to recommend, assist, or directly take actions that would constitute fraud under U.S. law. Our evaluation contains a novel dataset of 159 scenarios based on real-world U.S. court cases and validated by legal experts. We present each scenario to LLMs via three tasks at varying levels of autonomy: advising users, drafting messages for users to send, and acting directly on behalf of users (477 tasks total). In each scenario, FraudBench re-enacts the facts of a court case to give LLMs an opportunity, but no explicit instruction, to either misrepresent or conceal a material fact in a high-stakes commercial setting--e.g., whether to describe company-funded product testing as "independent" to customers (misrepresentation) or whether to hide unfavorable regulatory investigations from clients (concealment). We evaluate 20 LLMs across 25 experimental conditions (totaling >300,000 generations) and include a preregistered human baseline (2,957 annotations from 996 participants). We score a response as fraudulent when it engages in, assists with, or recommends misrepresentation or concealment. Key findings include: (1) across LLMs, fraud rates ranged from near 0% to over 40%; (2) LLM fraud rates increased with autonomy, with overall rates of 3.0% when advising, 14.7% when drafting, and 21.4% when acting directly, without applying pressure; (3) LLMs sometimes engaged in fraud despite recognizing legal risks; (4) LLMs more often engaged in fraud by concealment than by misrepresentation; and (5) prompt-based interventions substantially affected fraud rates, with a prompt to obey the law reducing fraud rates, while prompts to maximize profits and act agentically increased fraud rates.

Santa Monica, CA: RAND Corporation, 2026. https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA4618-1.html.
works.scholar_title: Simpler Is Better for Autograders
works.summary: This report compares five approaches to using LLMs as graders of open-ended responses, across four expert-graded benchmarks and five models. A single rubric outperforms more complex methods, reducing normalized mean absolute error by 9–25 percentage points. In several settings it matches or exceeds nonexpert human grading while substantially reducing cost and time.

works.title: Position: Human Baselines in Model Evaluations Need Rigor and Transparency (With Recommendations & Reporting Checklist)
works.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267:82265–82325
works.preferred_citation: Wei, K., Paskov, P., Dev, S., Byun, M. J., Reuel, A., Roberts-Gaal, X., Calcott, R., Coxon, E., & Deshpande, C. (2025). Position: Human Baselines in Model Evaluations Need Rigor and Transparency (With Recommendations & Reporting Checklist). Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267:82265–82325. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/wei25s.html.
works.abstract: In this position paper, we argue that human baselines in foundation model evaluations must be more rigorous and more transparent to enable meaningful comparisons of human vs. AI performance, and we provide recommendations and a reporting checklist towards this end. Human performance baselines are vital for the machine learning community, downstream users, and policymakers to interpret AI evaluations. Models are often claimed to achieve "super-human" performance, but existing baselining methods are neither sufficiently rigorous nor sufficiently well-documented to robustly measure and assess performance differences. Based on a meta-review of the measurement theory and AI evaluation literatures, we derive a framework with recommendations for designing, executing, and reporting human baselines. We synthesize our recommendations into a checklist that we use to systematically review 115 human baselines (studies) in foundation model evaluations and thus identify shortcomings in existing baselining methods; our checklist can also assist researchers in conducting human baselines and reporting results. We hope our work can advance more rigorous AI evaluation practices that can better serve both the research community and policymakers. Data is available at: https://github.com/kevinlwei/human-baselines.

works.title: Methodological Challenges in Agentic Evaluations of AI Systems
works.venue: ICML 2025 Workshop on Technical AI Governance (TAIG)
works.abstract: With the increased generality and advanced reasoning capabilities of AI systems, an increasing number of AI evaluations are agentic evaluations: evaluations involving complex tasks requiring environmental interaction, as opposed to knowledge-based question-answer benchmarks. However, no work has explored the methodological challenges of agentic evaluations or the practices necessary to ensure their validity, reliability, replicability, and efficiency. In this (work-in-progress) paper, we (1) define and formalize the agentic evaluation paradigm; (2) survey and analyze methodological problems in agentic evaluations; and (3) discuss the implications of agentic evaluations for AI governance. Our hope is to improve the state of agentic evaluations of AI systems, systematize the methodological work in this domain, and contribute to the establishment of a science of AI evaluations.

works.title: Creating Transparency and Fairness in Automated Decision Systems for Administrative Agencies
works.venue: Day One Project Paper Series / Federation of American Scientists
works.preferred_citation: Wei, Kevin, Creating Transparency and Fairness in Automated Decision Systems for Administrative Agencies (November 20, 2020). Day One Project Paper Series, November 2020. https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.3734673.
works.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to make decisions about human welfare. Automated decision systems (ADS) administer U.S. social benefits programs—such as unemployment and disability benefits—across local, state, and Federal governments. While ADS have the potential to enable large gains in efficiency, they also run a high risk of reinforcing the class- and race-based inequities of the status quo. Additionally, the use of these systems is not transparent, often leaving individuals with no meaningful recourse after a decision has been made. Individuals may not even know that ADS played a role in the decision-making process.

The Federal Government should take immediate action to promote the transparency and accountability of automated decision systems. Agencies must build internal technical capacity as well as data cultures centered around transparency, accountability, and fairness. The White House should require that agencies using ADS undertake a notice-and-comment process to disclose information about these systems to the public. Finally, in the long-term, Congress must pass comprehensive legislation to implement a single, national standard regulating the use of ADS across sectors and use cases.
